newsitem.title: UK: Calf has 10 pct risk of madcow disease - UK scientist.
newsitem.headline: Calf has 10 pct risk of madcow disease - UK scientist.

text.p: There is a one in 10 risk of a calf developing mad cow disease if it was born to a mother which incubated the disease, a British scientist working on an official report on the disease said on Tuesday.

British farmers' leaders said the news confirmed the threat posed by mad cow disease was receding. But it remained unclear whether the discovery would accelerate the ending of the ban on British beef exports.

Professor Roy Anderson, part of a team preparing a report for the Agriculture Ministry on mad cow disease -- Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) -- said the risk of maternal transmission was worst just before the calf's mother succumbs to the disease.
"There is an enhanced risk of a calf born to a mother who subsequently develops BSE itself developing BSE," Anderson said on BBC television.

"That risk is about 10 percent if you take it across the entire incubation period of the disease in the mother, which is five years, but the really enhanced risk occurs in the last 150 days prior to the mother going down with BSE."
While the report confirms that calves can contract BSE from their mothers, it is not yet clear how this happens, whether in the womb or from the cow's milk.

The study, on which scientists began work after BSE was first identified in 1986, is not expected to affect the time it will take to eradicate mad cow disease from British herds. Some scientists have forecast the disease will virtually disappear by 2001.

The President of Britain's National Farmers' Union, Sir David Naish, said: "I think consumers should accept now as a result of this research that British beef is safe, that fears of maternal transmission have receded a little."
The Ministry of Agriculture said it would not comment on the report until it was completed next month. "There is still work being done," a ministry spokeswoman said.

The European Union imposed a worldwide ban on British beef exports in March last year after the British government admitted a possible link between eating beef and developing Creuzfeldt-Jakob Disease, a brain disease that is invariably fatal.
At the EU summit in Florence last June, agreement was reached on phasing out the ban on British beef exports once EU experts were satisfied with measures Britain was to take to eradicate BSE.
